Well here's what our society needs to look like in the **long run**, let's say 50 years from now.  I'm basing this off of an interview I listened to, which featured an environmental economist who had worked on a report, looking at what it would take for a North American country to reduce emissions by 90%:

-Electricity must be almost 100% provided by non-emitting sources, meaning hydro, nuclear, solar, wind, and geothermal.  Currently I believe we're in the 70-80% range, so this is actually very achievable, but it'll mean we need much more power from those sources (obviously) and will need to better connect the electric grids between regions.  For example, a western province's grid may need more connections with an inland province's to help them eliminate coal use.

-Personal transportation will need to be almost entirely electric-powered.  Public transit systems, electric cars, and maybe hybrids.

-For freight transportation, electric batteries might not be able to provide enough power, so biofuels could be the best solution here.

-Heating systems for buildings should be powered by electricity, instead of natural gas

-Heavy industries and factories will be the most difficult, since a factory that is built can last 50+ years, rather than being replaced every couple decades like vehicles are, so in 2065 we will still have factories and equipment that were built in 2015.  So adding carbon-capture-and-storage (CCS) may be the most practical option in many cases, so that the industries still create emissions, but those emissions would be re-directed to be buried deep underground

In terms of public policy needed to achieve this vision, the most important thing is to have a carbon tax, so that polluting is no longer free and must be taken into account in business (and personal) decision-making.  And that carbon tax should steadily increase, to create more and more incentives for people to innovate and transition away from highly-polluting activities and fuel sources.

The good thing about carbon taxes (rather than a more heavy-handed regulatory approach) is that it allows individuals and businesses in the market to decide for themselves what the most cost-effective way of reducing their emissions would be.  Because sure, we can sketch out how we envision our clean-energy society looking in 2065, as I did above, but the future is dynamic and people might find more efficient ways of reducing those emissions sources than the ways I outlined.  So using a carbon tax, rather than top-down regulations that require specific changes, allows them the flexibility to find the best approaches.

Well it was first implemented in 2008 as a $10/tonne of CO2 tax, and then it increased yearly to $15, $20, $25 and then $30/tonne, which is the rate that it is currently frozen at.  The current $30/tonne tax adds 6.7 cents to the price of a litre of gasoline, and [applies to other fuel sources as well](http://www.fin.gov.bc.ca/tbs/tp/climate/A4.htm), with tax rates based on the amount of CO2 that they create.  Currently the tax applies to [70% of all of BC's emissions](http://www.fin.gov.bc.ca/tbs/tp/climate/A6.htm), since it would be more difficult to apply the tax to non-fuel-related agricultural emissions or deforestation.

BC carbon tax has been billed as [revenue-neutral](http://www.fin.gov.bc.ca/tbs/tp/climate/tax_cuts.htm), because all revenue from the tax has been returned to the public in the form of [other tax cuts and grants](http://www.fin.gov.bc.ca/tbs/tp/climate/A2.htm).  More specifically, the revenue has been used to reduce income taxes, reduce corporate taxes, send a tax-rebate to all low-income residents 4x a year (along with GST rebates), and provide a grant to all rural residents.

The key concept and reasoning behind the carbon tax, is that air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions are a [negative externality](http://www.economicsonline.co.uk/Market_failures/Externalities.html), which harms other parties, but will not be properly taken into account in an individual's decision-making.  This results in a market failure, where markets will over-produce goods which cause harm to people outside of the transaction (everyone other than the buyer or the seller), since the buyer and seller will be acting in their own self-interest, and not fully considering their impact on everyone else.  The carbon tax is meant to account for those external impacts, to bring an individual's private costs of polluting more in line with the full costs to society.

Here's a Globe and Mail article about BC's carbon tax: http://www.theglobeandmail.com/globe-debate/the-insidious-truth-about-bcs-carbon-tax-it-works/article19512237/

>At the same time, it’s been extraordinarily effective in tackling the root cause of carbon pollution: the burning of fossil fuels. Since the tax came in, fuel use in B.C. has dropped by 16 per cent; in the rest of Canada, it’s risen by 3 per cent (counting all fuels covered by the tax). To put that accomplishment in perspective, Canada’s Kyoto target was a 6-per-cent reduction in 20 years. And the evidence points to the carbon tax as the major driver of these B.C. gains.

The debate between ward-based and at-large voting systems presents a complex set of trade-offs. Ward systems offer more localized representation, but they can encourage councillors to prioritize their specific neighborhoods over the broader community, potentially fostering NIMBYism and inter-neighborhood political conflict. Conversely, at-large voting encourages a broader perspective, yet it can disadvantage independent or lesser-known candidates running on grassroots platforms and may reduce the sense of direct representation for individual constituents.

Ultimately, there is no clear consensus on the superior model. While the current at-large system is appreciated for minimizing hyper-local politics and enabling councillors to focus on city-wide priorities, the merits of a ward-based approach are also recognized. Concerns remain that the current system overwhelms voters with too many candidates, which can negatively impact voter engagement and the effectiveness of local representation.

Historically, this issue has been the subject of five referendums or plebiscites since 1970:

> 1973: 59 per cent of voters chose to maintain the at-large system.

> 1978: 52 per cent voted in favor of reinstating a ward system. However, amendments to the provincial legislation governing the city specified that any change to the electoral system required a 60 per cent majority vote in a referendum.

> 1988: 56 per cent voted in favor of wards, falling short of the required 60 per cent threshold.

> 1996: 59 per cent voted in favor of keeping the at-large system.

> 2004: 54 per cent voted against adopting a ward system.

>I find it interesting that most people arguing against a referendum are basically arguing against democracy.

Not at all.  Voting for a representative is very different from voting on a specific topic.

Most people are interested and knowledgeable about *some* topics, but very few people are interested and knowledgeable about *every* topic.  When voting for political parties and representatives, people can use the issues that they know and care most about to decide which party best matches their views and values.

So for example, if I know lots about economic and environmental policy, but only have a shallow understanding of foreign policy, it's okay because I can judge the parties based on their economic and environmental policies, which are issues that I do understand.

However with a referendum, we're relying on *everyone* to be knowledgeable, interested, and informed about the same topic.  If it's a topic with any complexity (like electoral reform), then that won't necessarily work very well, because let's be honest: most people are not going to approach the topic with an open mind and spend 3+ hours independently researching it, and weighing the tradeoffs and potential implications.  Most will hear about it on the news a few times, hear an argument that they like, and vote accordingly.  This also makes it very easy for many people to be convinced by misleading information, because they're not experts on the topic, and most people don't have the time or interest to develop a very thorough understanding of the topic before voting.

Basically the European countries in the Schengen Area have no border controls between themselves, so people and goods can move freely between them without any waits, and without needing to bring a passport.  So for example, you can drive or take a train from a Western European nation to a neighboring one to another neighboring one to a Central European one without going through any border stops, or you can fly between those countries without going through customs.  It also speeds up goods movement, since trucks and freight trains don't have to wait in border lines and get searched every time they cross a national border.

However there are still border stops and customs for entering or leaving the Schengen Area (so going from a North American nation to a Western European nation you still need a passport and must clear customs, obviously).

The upsides are easier travel, more efficient trade, etc.  Downsides are that each country has less control over who or what goods enter their country, so they have to establish some common rules and regulations that apply to all countries in the Schengen Area, and they also have to count of the other countries in the Schengen Area to be secure.
